translator: Claude (AI), draft, not reviewed by a Hittitologist
intro: KUB 9.31 is the best-preserved copy of a tablet that collects three rituals against epidemic: the ritual of Zarpiya, physician of Kizzuwatna (§0–21), the ritual of Uḫḫamuwa of Arzawa (§22–25) and the ritual of Ašḫella of Ḫapalla (§26–34), followed by a colophon listing all three (§35). It duplicates KBo 13.212+, but preserves the opening of Zarpiya's ritual, an episode with eight boys and a 'wolf' howl, a Luwian invocation of Šanta and the full second day of Ašḫella's ritual, all lost or only partly preserved in the duplicate.

sections.title: Ritual of Zarpiya, physician of Kizzuwatna
Ritual of Uḫḫamuwa, man of Arzawa
Ritual of Ašḫella, man of Ḫapalla, and colophon

paras.en: [Thus (says) Zarp]iya, physician of Kizzuwat[na]: [If] the [yea]r is bad (and) there is continual dying in the land, (and) [the plag]ue(?) is bad(?) behind(?) whichever city, [then] the master of the house does as follows:

[The master of the ritu]al(?) hangs up (text: 'I hang up') a kelu-(?). On it (is) a bronze ḫuppali-(?); its [hoo]d(?) (is) of the skin of a shaggy(?) lion(?); its [footstool(?)] (is) of kunkunuzzi-stone, and its ḫazziul-(?) [of] lapis lazuli; a šišai-(?); a strong(?) šišai-(?) of a bear(?); and he hangs up (that) of a wild goat(?).

And an aleš-(?) of black wool, red wool, ḫarnuwašila-(?) (wool) and gr[een] wool, and dog's sinew … opposite … šakaltan(?); and them […] three times(?). On one side (he hangs) one on a peg of medlar(?) wood, and on the other side one on [a peg] of cornel(?) wood.

And in front, on the front side, in the gate, on the one side(?) he drives in (lit. strikes) a peg of medlar(?) wood, and he hangs (on it) a cooked [kukk]ulla-(cake) of barley flour and a [kukk]ulla-(cake) of ḫariyant-(?) barley [fl]our, (and) one jug of wine. On the other side of the ga[te] he drives in [a peg] of cornel(?) wood, and he hangs (on it) a cooked ku[kkulla-(cake)] of barley flour, a ḫariyant-(?) kukkulla-(cake) and one jug of wine.

Below the pegs white(?) ḫa[ḫḫal]-greenery is stuck in. Below, from the ground, below the [a]šara-(?), in front, on this side and on [that side] he buries(?) a remedy(?): ḫuwallari (is its) name. [Then], in whichever gate (it is), he hangs the kelamu-(?) be[hind the door] of the courtyard. In front, below, he sets up one wicker table of the kilawa-(ritual). On it he places a bronze axe, one warm loaf, one thick loaf (and) cheese; and on top he places a bronze axe, a bronze dagger, a drawn bow (and) one arrow.
In front, below, at the wicker table he places one bowl of wine [on a tr]ay, and he places one jug of (beer-)drink on a tray; into the jug of drink he sets one drinking straw.

[And] they drive up [one] billy goat, and the master of the house offers it [befo]re the table w[ith] wine to Šanta. [And] he holds out the bro[nze] axe and speaks thus: 'Come, Šanta! [And] with you let the Innarawant-(deities) come, who are clothed in bloodied (garments), who have bound on the ḫupru- of the lulaḫi-men,

who are girded with daggers, who have their bows drawn and [hol]d arrows! Come and eat!' And w[hen] he finishes speaking the oath(?), he sets his axe down [on] the table, and they [stab] the billy goat.

He takes the blood […] [the straw that] is set [in the j]ug (of drink), and [he smears] it […]. The liver […] they [bri]ng, and he [hold]s it (out) (to) the master [of the house …]. Then […] to the st[raw …], and he si[ps …].

[… (the lost end of column I probably contained the oath speech, the cooking of the liver and heart and the laying out of the meat, as preserved in the duplicate KBo 13.212+) …] [… Sun-go]d, e[a]t! Let the father-gods of the house eat! Let the Thousand Gods eat!

And be witnesses to this oath!' Afterwards he libates wine nine times before the table of the Innarawant-(deities); he places the shoulder and the breast on it, and he breaks up the nine thick loaves.

He heaps them on the laḫḫura-(offering table), and opposite (it) he pours wine. Then they bring eight boys who have not yet gone to a woman. They clothe one boy in the skin of a billy goat, and he walks in front and calls out like a wolf. They turn the tables around(?), and they eat up the shoulder and the breast.
But for eating […] … good, and he brings (it) likewise, and they eat up the [liver and the heart]. They drink […], and they also dri[nk] the jug of (beer-)drink.
The master of the house [takes(?)] a staff of šuruḫḫa-wood […], steps into the gate, and conjures in Luwian as follows:

[Luwian:] 'Šanta, the king, (and) the Annarumi-(deities), who are clothed in bloodied (garments)(?), who have bound on the ḫuppara- of the Lulaḫi-(men)(?) …' (the wording closely parallels the Hittite invocation in §6)
[Luwian incantation, only partly understood: '… foot(?) back(?) … with evil(?) … do not … sheep, cattle, human being … do not eat(?)!']
He breaks a thick loaf and speaks as follows in Luwian:
[Luwian incantation, not securely understood: '(O) great(?) Sun-god, father-gods, … Ea(?) … into the house(?) … when(?) … they take(?) …']
[Luwian lines naming the god Ea(?) (the duplicate writes A.A), not understood.]
They take up the ritual implements, and he closes the door, anoints it with fine oil and speaks:
'Let evil be shut out(?); let good be held fast(?) inside!'

[Colophon of the first ritual:] One long tablet, complete: the word of Zarpiya, physician of the land of Kizzuwatna. If the year is bad (and) there is continual dying in the land, he offers the kilu-(ritual) as follows.
Thus (says) Uḫḫamuwa, man of Arzawa: If there is continual dying in the land, and if some god of the enemy has caused it, then I do as follows:

They drive up two(?) rams (the duplicate has one). They twist together blue wool, red wool, yellow(-green) wool, black wool and white wool, and make [i]t into a crown, and they crown one ram. They drive the one ram out onto the road of the enemy, and while doing so they speak thus: 'Whatever god of the enemy land has caused [this pla]gue, see, we have driven [this] crowned ram to you, the god, [for pe]ace. And just as a (city) wall is [fir]m (the duplicate has: 'a knot'), (so) he is at peace(?) with this ram. But you, whatever god has caused [this pl]ague, be likewise at peace with the land of Ḫattuša, and [tu]rn again in favour toward the land of Ḫattuša!' And they drive the one crowned ram away [into] the enemy land.

Afterwards they bring fodder and tallow for the god's horses, and they speak thus about it: 'You have harnessed the horses; let them eat this fodder and be sated. And let your chariot be greased with tallow. O god, Storm-god, turn back into your (own) land, but toward the land of Ḫattuša turn in favour!'

Afterwards they drive up one billy goat (and) two sheep (the duplicate: 'are killed'). He offers the billy goat to the Seven (Sebettu), and one sheep he offers to the Sun-god (not in the duplicate); one sheep they kill and cook. Then they bring one cheese, one sour (loaf), one pulla-vessel of sour bread, one bowl of wine, one bowl of beer and fruit, and they prepare them for the god of the road.
Thus (says) Ašḫella, man of Ḫapalla: If in the land […] or in the army camp there is dying, then [I perform] this ri[tual]:

I take the following: when on (that) day it comes to evening time, whoever are the lords of the [ar]my, al[l] of them, each one prepares a ram for himself — whether the rams are white or dark does not matter at all. And I twist together a cord of white wool, red wool (and) green wool, and he plaits it into one, and I set into it one [bead(?) and one] ring of iron and of lead, and I bind it onto the necks and horns of the rams. At night they tie them up in front of the tents, and while doing so they speak thus: 'Whatever god is roaming about [be]low, whatever god has caused this plague: […] see, I have tied up these rams; be appeased!'

[In the morni]ng I drive them to the open country, and with eac[h] […] [r]am they [bri]ng one jug, one thick loaf (and) one cup of fired clay. In front of the king's tent he seats a [deco]rated woman, and one bowl of beer (and) three thick [loaves] […] he places beside the [wom]an.

Then the lords of the army place their hands on the rams, and they speak thus: 'Whatever god has caused this plague, now see, the rams are standing (here), and they are very fat in liver, heart and loins. Let human flesh be hateful to him henceforth(?), and be appeased by these rams!' The lords of the army bow down behind the rams, and the king bows down behind the decorated woman.

Then they carry the rams, the woman, the thick loaves and the beer away through the middle of the army camp and drive them to the open country. They go and let them loose into the enemy's border(-land), to a place where our (people) do not go. And there they speak just so: 'See, whatever evil of this army camp was in human beings, cattle, sheep, horses, mules and donkeys — now see, these rams and the woman have carried it away from [the army camp]. [Whoever] finds them, let that land take this evil plague for itself!'

On the second day, when it grows light in the early morning, they qu[ickly] prepare six rams, six billy goats, twelve GÌR.GÁN-vessels, twelve cups, twelve thick loaves (the duplicate perhaps has fourteen), one bowl of beer (and) three small bronze knives, and they drive them to the open country, again to another place; and they carry all this along with (them). When they bring them to the open country, they slaughter them on the ground and cook them plainly. They spread leafy branches underneath, and on (them) the fat (and) the thick loaves […] […] […] […]. Then [they …] fire […] they kindle, and they come a[way] through the middle of [it]. At the fr[ont(?)] they prepare two billy goats, one bowl of wine (and) five thick loaves, and he offers the two billy goats to the Tutelary Deity of the aniyatta-(field equipment?). He places the breast, the right shoulder, the liver (and) the heart, cooked, on leafy branches, and he drinks (to) the Tutelary Deity of the aniyatta- (… ḫalziyaš, unclear) three times. They eat, and they come away. (At this point the duplicate has an offering speech, a rule about implements and a hand-washing with salt water; KUB 9.31 preserves only traces.)

On the third day, when it grows li[gh]t in the early mo[rning], they quickly drive up one billy goat, one [r]am and one pig, and behind (them) they prepare three thick loaves and one bowl of beer, and they drive them to the open country, again to another place. They spread out leafy branches and place the three thick loaves on the leafy branches. They offer the billy goat, the ram and the pig to [that] god, (saying): 'Whatever [god] has made this plague in the army cam[p], let that [god] eat and drink, and let him [be] at peace with the land of Ḫattuša and with the ar[my] of Ḫattuša, and let him turn inward in favour!' They eat and drink, and they come away.

On the fourth day, when it grows light in the early morning, they quickly drive up a bull, one ewe (and) three rams — a ewe to which a ram has not yet gone — and ten thick loaves, one bowl of beer and one bowl of wine, and they drive them to the open country, again to another place. He offers the bull to the Storm-god,

and he offers the ewe to the Sun-god, and they offer the three sheep to all the gods. They spread leafy branches [on the gro]und, and he sets back (on them) the breast, the right [shoulder], the liver, the heart and the thick loaves, cooked; and he drinks three times (to) the Sun-god of Heaven, the Storm-god and all the [god]s. They eat, and they come away.

[Colophon:] One tablet: on it three rituals are set down. One ritual, the word of Zarpiya: if the year is bad, how they perform the kilawa-ritual. One ritual, the word of Uḫḫamuwa: if there is continual dying in the land or the city. One ritual, the word of Ašḫella: if there is dying in the land or in the army [camp]s.
